description: Safeguarding procedures: policies, the DSL role, staff training and DBS checks.
content_html:
What Is Safeguarding?

Safeguarding is the responsibility every care setting has to protect the people in its care from harm. It is not a single action but a system — involving policies, trained staff, designated leads and background checks — that works together to create a safe environment. This lesson covers section 4.1 of the spec: who needs safeguarding, the impacts when it is absent, and the specific procedures that settings must have in place.

It is important to approach this topic calmly and factually. The purpose of learning about safeguarding is to understand how to recognise signs of concern and respond correctly by reporting to the right person — not to investigate or challenge alone. Every care worker’s most important safeguarding action is knowing who to tell and telling them promptly.

Key Fact

Safeguarding is especially important for vulnerable groups: children, older adults in residential care, people with physical or learning disabilities, people with mental health conditions, people with a sensory impairment, homeless people, and people dependent on carers for daily support.

Service Users Who Need Safeguarding

Some individuals are more vulnerable than others because their circumstances make it harder for them to recognise, report or escape a situation where they are at risk of harm. The spec lists seven groups, and it is worth understanding why each group is vulnerable — this helps with application questions in the exam.

Children may not fully understand that what is happening to them is wrong, or may feel unable to tell a trusted adult. Older adults in residential care may be dependent on carers for every aspect of daily life, making it difficult to raise concerns. People with physical or learning disabilities may have difficulty communicating concerns or may be reliant on the people who support them. People with mental health conditions may find their accounts dismissed or may have reduced capacity to make decisions at certain times. People who have a sensory impairment — such as sight loss or hearing loss — may have limited access to information or reduced ability to raise the alarm. Homeless people may be in precarious situations with less access to formal support, and may not know where to seek help. People in residential care dependent on carers are particularly reliant on the goodwill and professionalism of those caring for them.

Impacts of a Lack of Safeguarding

When safeguarding procedures are absent, inadequate or not followed, the consequences for a service user can be serious and far-reaching. The spec asks you to know the PIES impacts of a lack of safeguarding.

Physical impacts can include injury, illness, malnutrition or worsening health. For example, if an older adult in a care home is not being helped to eat and drink adequately — a form of neglect — they may become dehydrated and physically unwell. Intellectual impacts include a lack of mental stimulation, loss of concentration, or failure to receive education that a child is entitled to. Emotional impacts can include depression, low self-esteem, anxiety, distress and feelings of worthlessness. A young person in a residential setting who is not safeguarded appropriately may become withdrawn and unable to trust adults. Social impacts include isolation, difficulty forming relationships, and reduced participation in community life.

It is worth noting that these PIES impacts rarely occur in isolation. A service user experiencing harm may feel emotionally distressed (E), which causes them to withdraw from social interactions (S), which in turn reduces their intellectual stimulation (I) and can lead to physical deterioration through loss of appetite (P). Making these connections between PIES is exactly what the exam rewards at the higher mark bands.

Students sometimes write that confidentiality is absolute — that information about a service user must never be shared. This is incorrect in a safeguarding context. Confidentiality is an important right, but the right to protection from abuse and harm takes priority when there is a serious concern about safety. If a child tells a teaching assistant at an after-school club that someone at home is hurting them, the teaching assistant is obliged to report this to the Designated Safeguarding Lead — even if the child asks them not to tell anyone. The practitioner should tell the child honestly that they need to share this information with a person who can help. Safeguarding always overrides confidentiality where there is a risk to life or safety.

Safeguarding Procedures in Care Settings

The spec requires you to know four key safeguarding procedures: the safeguarding policy, the Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL), safeguarding training, and DBS checks.

A safeguarding policy is the formal written document that sets out everyone’s responsibilities. It tells staff what to do if they have a concern, who to report to, and what records to keep. Without a policy, staff may be unsure of their responsibilities and concerns may fall through the gaps.

The DSL is a named individual — often a senior member of staff — who is specifically trained to receive and act on safeguarding concerns. In a school, this is typically the deputy headteacher or a senior teacher. In a residential care home, it may be the registered manager. The DSL is the person every other staff member should report concerns to. They then decide whether to refer the concern to external agencies such as children’s services or the police. The DSL role ensures that safeguarding is coordinated and not left to individual staff to manage alone.

Key Fact

The four safeguarding procedures are: safeguarding policy (written responsibilities and reporting pathways), DSL (named lead who receives and coordinates concerns), safeguarding training (ensures all staff know signs of harm and reporting routes), and DBS checks (background checks on all staff before they work with vulnerable groups).

Safeguarding Training and the Duty to Report

All staff in a care setting — not just the DSL — must receive safeguarding training. Training ensures that every member of staff can: recognise possible signs of harm or abuse (such as unexplained injuries, changes in behaviour, or a service user appearing frightened or distressed around a particular person); know the setting’s procedures for reporting a concern or disclosure; understand their personal duty to report; and know who the DSL is and how to contact them. The spec is explicit: the training is for all staff, because any member of staff may be the first person a service user chooses to tell.

DBS Checks

Before any staff member works with vulnerable groups, they must undergo a DBS check through the Disclosure and Barring Service. There are three types, and your exam requires you to know the difference between them.

A standard DBS check reveals spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings from the Police National Computer. An enhanced DBS check includes all the information in a standard check plus any additional relevant information held by local police forces that they believe is relevant to the role. For roles involving regular unsupervised contact with children or vulnerable adults — such as a care worker, nurse, teacher or foster carer — an enhanced check is required, and it will also include a check of the barred list: a register of people who are legally prohibited from working with children or vulnerable adults.

A common exam question asks you to distinguish the three types of DBS check. A simple way to think about it: Standard = Police National Computer records (convictions, cautions). Enhanced = Standard + anything relevant held by local police. Barred list = a separate, specific register of people banned from working with vulnerable groups. In a care role, you need an enhanced check WITH barred list — that is the highest level of check available and it is required for anyone working directly and unsupervised with children or vulnerable adults. The barred list is not a level of DBS check on its own; it is an addition to the enhanced check. Getting this distinction right is worth marks in a short-answer question.
exam_tip_html: Safeguarding appears most often as a 4-mark Describe question (applied to a named scenario) or an 8-mark Discuss / Evaluate question. For a 4-mark Describe: the question will give you a named setting and service user and ask you to describe safeguarding procedures or impacts. Tie every point to a feature of the named scenario — mark schemes credit answers that link a procedure to the specific setting or service user type. For the 8-mark Discuss: you will need to analyse the impacts of a lack of safeguarding AND evaluate the effectiveness of procedures. Use PIES to structure your analysis of impacts, and show that you understand how the procedures (policy, DSL, training, DBS) work together as a system. A common error is writing about safeguarding generally without connecting it back to the specific group mentioned in the question — always reference the vulnerability of the named service user. Avoid using graphic descriptions when discussing harm; factual, neutral language focused on recognition and reporting earns full marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Safeguarding protects vulnerable groups — including children, older adults, people with disabilities, sensory impairments or mental health conditions, and homeless people — from harm. Vulnerability is linked to dependency, difficulty communicating, or limited access to support.
  • A lack of safeguarding produces PIES impacts: physical harm, intellectual disadvantage, emotional distress and social isolation — and these connect to each other in chains that extended-response answers should trace.
  • The four key safeguarding procedures are the safeguarding policy, the DSL, training for all staff, and DBS checks. The three DBS check types — standard (convictions), enhanced (standard + police intelligence), and barred list (prohibited persons) — must be clearly distinguished in your exam answers.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what a standard DBS check reveals?
A) Spent and unspent convictions plus any information held by local police
B) Only unspent convictions
C) Spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings
D) Whether a person is on the barred list
practice_questions.marks: C) Spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two groups of people who may need safeguarding in health and social care settings.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each group named with a brief reason or characteristic, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: children (may not recognise harm or be unable to report it); older adults in residential care (dependent on carers, may have limited capacity to raise concerns); people with physical or learning disabilities (may have difficulty communicating concerns); people with mental health conditions (may have reduced capacity at times or accounts may be questioned); people with sensory impairment such as sight or hearing loss (limited access to information or support); homeless people (precarious circumstances, limited access to formal support). A one-word group name without any characteristic earns 0.

practice_questions.text: Describe two emotional impacts on a service user when safeguarding is not in place.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described emotional impact, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: depression or persistent low mood; low self-esteem or feeling worthless or inadequate; anxiety or fear; distress and upset; anger or frustration; feeling unable to trust adults or practitioners. A single word (e.g. 'sad') without description of characteristics earns 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain why safeguarding training is important for all staff in a residential care home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that training ensures all staff know the signs of harm; 1 mark for explaining why this matters (e.g. because any staff member may be the first person a service user chooses to disclose to, so all staff need to know the reporting procedure); 1 mark for explaining the outcome with a 'therefore' or 'this means that' chain (e.g. therefore concerns are reported quickly and consistently, reducing the risk of ongoing harm to the service user). No third mark without reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Priya manages a 20-place residential care home for adults with learning disabilities. A new care worker, 22-year-old Tomasz, has just started on the support team. The setting also works with volunteers who help with activities twice a week.

Describe four safeguarding procedures the residential care home should have in place to protect its service users.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described procedure, up to 4 marks. Acceptable answers include: a safeguarding policy setting out responsibilities, reporting pathways and what staff should do if they have a concern; a named Designated Safeguarding Lead to receive and coordinate concerns; safeguarding training for all staff (including new starters like Tomasz) so they can recognise signs of harm and know reporting routes; DBS checks (enhanced with barred list) completed before Tomasz or any volunteer begins work with service users. Answers that name a procedure without describing what it does earn 0 for that mark.

practice_questions.text:
A children's charity runs an after-school club and Saturday sports programme at a community centre. The club has 30 children aged 7-11 including some with physical disabilities and one child whose parent has recently raised a concern about unexplained bruising.

Discuss the importance of safeguarding procedures in the children's charity's setting, and evaluate how effectively these procedures protect the children in the club.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Response discusses the importance of each safeguarding procedure (policy, DSL, training, DBS) with clear reasoning about why each is necessary in the named setting. Applies to the specific vulnerabilities of the service users (children, some with disabilities). Analyses the impacts of inadequate safeguarding using PIES with at least one connection between categories. Reaches an evaluative judgement, for example weighing whether procedures alone are sufficient or whether staff culture and training quality also matter. Uses precise terminology (safeguarding policy, DSL, standard/enhanced DBS, barred list, duty to report, disclosure).

Secure (5-6 marks): Covers most procedures with mostly accurate application. Refers to the named setting and the specific vulnerability of children. Some PIES analysis of impacts. Mostly developed points. May lack a final judgement or have one under-developed PIES connection.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant content about safeguarding procedures but limited development. May list procedures without explaining their importance. Limited or no PIES analysis. Some reference to the scenario.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge about safeguarding with little or no application to a named setting, vulnerable group, or procedural framework. Listing rather than discussing or evaluating.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes the role of the Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL)?
options: The person who carries out DBS checks on new staff
The named trained person responsible for receiving and coordinating safeguarding concerns
The manager who writes the safeguarding policy
The person who decides whether a concern requires police involvement without involving anyone else

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of DBS check reveals spent and unspent convictions AND additional information held by local police?
In a safeguarding context, a care worker's most important immediate action when a service user discloses a concern is to _____ the Designated Safeguarding Lead.
People who are dependent on carers for daily support are considered _____ because they may find it difficult to raise concerns about those who care for them.
Match each DBS check type to what it reveals:
right: Spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings
Standard check information plus relevant local police intelligence
Whether a person is legally prohibited from working with vulnerable groups

flashcard_questions.a: The measures and procedures care settings use to protect vulnerable individuals from harm, abuse or neglect.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three groups of people who may need safeguarding in care settings.
flashcard_questions.a: Any three of: children; older adults in residential care; people with physical or learning disabilities; people with mental health conditions; people with sensory impairment; homeless people.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are people dependent on carers considered a vulnerable group for safeguarding purposes?
flashcard_questions.a: They rely on carers for daily support, making it difficult to raise concerns about the people caring for them.

flashcard_questions.q: Name four safeguarding procedures a care setting should have in place.
flashcard_questions.a: Safeguarding policy; Designated Safeguarding Lead; safeguarding training for all staff; DBS checks for all staff.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the DSL in a care setting?
flashcard_questions.a: To receive, coordinate and act on safeguarding concerns reported by other staff members.

flashcard_questions.q: What does safeguarding training ensure all staff can do?
flashcard_questions.a: Recognise signs of harm, know reporting procedures, know their duty to report, and know who the DSL is.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a standard DBS check reveal?
flashcard_questions.a: Spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings from the Police National Computer.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an enhanced DBS check reveal that a standard check does not?
flashcard_questions.a: Additional relevant information held by local police forces alongside the standard check information.
A list of people legally prohibited from working with children or vulnerable adults, checked as part of an enhanced DBS.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two emotional impacts a service user may experience if safeguarding is not in place.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: depression; low self-esteem; anxiety; distress; anger or frustration; inability to trust others.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does safeguarding training need to cover all staff, not just the DSL?
flashcard_questions.a: Any staff member may be the first person a service user chooses to disclose a concern to.

flashcard_questions.q: When does safeguarding override the right to confidentiality?
flashcard_questions.a: When there is a serious concern about a service user's safety — protection from harm takes priority.

glossary_terms.definition: The range of measures, procedures and responsibilities that health and social care settings put in place to protect vulnerable individuals from harm, abuse or neglect.
The named, trained member of staff in a care or education setting who is responsible for coordinating all safeguarding concerns and referrals.
The formal written document in a care setting that sets out responsibilities, procedures and reporting pathways for protecting service users from harm.
A Disclosure and Barring Service background check on a person's criminal history, used to help employers decide whether someone is suitable to work with children or vulnerable adults.
A background check that reveals spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings held on the Police National Computer.
A background check that includes all standard DBS information plus any additional relevant information held by local police forces.
A list maintained by the Disclosure and Barring Service of individuals who are legally prohibited from working with children or vulnerable adults.

People whose circumstances make them more likely to need protection from harm, including children, older adults in care, people with disabilities, and those with mental health conditions or sensory impairments.

hero_image_caption: Safeguarding is a shared responsibility — every member of staff in a care setting has a duty to protect the people in their care.
